unit.title: Filter the Clarity dashboard to a roughly six-month sample period

claim.text: The source says the first thing it does on the main Clarity dashboard is filter for a good enough sample size or sample period.
claim.quote: filter for a good enough sample size or good enough sample period

action.text: Set the dashboard date range to roughly the last 6 months of data, or last 90 days of data; historical availability varies with when Clarity was set up.
action.quote: typically that's going to be the last 6 months of data it could also be last 90 days of data

args.text: Opening the main Clarity dashboard to review metrics.
args.quote: the first thing that I like to do when looking at the main dashboard

args.text: Clarity must have been set up long enough ago to retain the desired window; the source says this varies by account.
args.quote: depending on when you set up Clarity you may or may not have the ability to go that far back

completion.text: The window selected is roughly six months; the exact boundary does not have to match.
completion.quote: so roughly 6 months doesn't have to be exact

unknowns: The source calls 6 months generally good while also offering last 90 days, without a rule for choosing between them.

unit.title: Prioritize the Insights block over baseline KPIs on the main dashboard

claim.text: The source identifies the Insights block as the part of the main dashboard that is important to focus on.
claim.quote: the part that I find is important to focus on on the main dashboard is really this insights block here

args.text: Most other dashboard metrics can be pulled from Google Analytics and are not unique to Clarity.
args.quote: a lot of the metrics on the main Clarity dashboard you can actually pull directly from Google analytics

unknowns: The named baseline KPIs (scroll depth, active time, pages per session, total sessions) are described as obtainable elsewhere, not as unusable.

unit.title: Open recordings from the rage-click insight's camera icon and watch them

claim.text: The source says watching the matching recordings is worthwhile when a rage-click metric warrants a particular change, to see where people hit frustration or friction.
claim.quote: if the rage clicks actually warrant particular change then it's worth watching those recordings to see you know where people experiencing frustration or friction

action.text: Click the camera icon next to the rage-click insight to open the recordings page, then watch the recordings of people who experienced rage clicks.
action.quote: you can actually click on this little camera icon and it's going to open up the recordings page where you can watch the actual recordings of people that experienced the rage clicks

args.text: The rage-click insight warrants a particular change.
args.quote: if the rage clicks actually warrant particular change

unknowns: The source's fuller recordings walkthrough is promised later in the video and is not in this passage.

unit.title: Author's heuristic range for an acceptable rage-click rate

claim.text: The source offers a heuristic that anything under 1 to 2 percent is good.
claim.quote: I would say anything really under 1 to two% is good

unknowns: This is presented as the author's heuristic, not a verified platform benchmark.
The denominator for the rate is not defined in this passage.

unit.title: Consider watching recordings across insight types even when metrics look low

claim.text: The source says it does not really matter what the metrics are; fundamental usability issues existing on the site should be resolved regardless of the percentage.
claim.quote: it doesn't really matter what the metrics are if there's usability issues fundamental that exist on the site ultimately you want to resolve them regardless of what the percentage is

action.text: Consider watching the recordings behind all of the insight metrics, not only the ones with high rates.
action.quote: again I would consider watching the recordings of all of these

args.text: An insight metric looks low, for example excessive scrolling under 0.01 percent, and appears not to be a major concern.
args.quote: in this particular scenario it's less than 0.01% so it's not really a major concern

unknowns: The source does not define what counts as a fundamental usability issue or how resolution is verified.

claim.text: The source has a sentence about spending time on dashboard metrics that overlap with Google Analytics, but the clause is garbled and its polarity is unresolved.
claim.quote: so I would really spend too much time there

args.text: Reviewing dashboard sections that overlap with Google Analytics.
args.quote: you can do all of this inside of Google analytics and a much better job at that as well

additions.title: Understand rage clicks as repeated clicking on an element to exit an experience

claim.text: The source defines rage clicks as people clicking multiple times on an element, typically to exit that experience.
claim.quote: rage clicking or clicking multiple times on an element typically to kind of exit that experience

unknowns: The source gives popup and chat-bot examples; no universal rate threshold is defined in this excerpt beyond the speaker's heuristic.

additions.title: Popup on first seconds can trigger rage clicks

claim.text: The source gives the example of a popup landing immediately in the first five seconds, when a user has barely scrolled and rage clicks to get rid of it.
claim.quote: you have a popup that lands immediately on the first 5 Seconds somebody's barely even scrolled on the site and they're just rage clicking trying to get rid of that popup

unknowns: The source does not quantify how often this pattern occurs.

additions.title: Chat bot blocking a form or add-to-cart can cause rage clicks

claim.text: The source gives the example of trying to exit a chat bot that prevents adding to cart or filling out a form and clicking submit on a B2B site.
claim.quote: trying to exit a chat bot that's preventing you from adding to card or filling out a form and clicking the submit button if it's a B2B site

unknowns: The source says this is generally low-hanging fruit but does not describe a specific fix.

additions.title: Understand quick backs as visitors rapidly returning to the previous page

claim.text: The source defines quick backs as people going to a page and then quickly returning to the previous one.
claim.quote: this is people where they're going to a page as cler saying right here and then they're quickly returning back to the previous one

unknowns: The source says the insight can indicate users could not find information immediately and are bouncing back and forth.

additions.title: Interpret quick backs as users not finding information immediately

claim.text: The source derives that users may be looking for information on a page but cannot find it immediately, so they bounce back and forth.
claim.quote: people are looking for information on a page but they're not able to find it immediately right so they have to constantly bounce back and forth

unknowns: The source gives a product page expectation as an example but does not prescribe a fix.

additions.title: Resolve fundamental usability issues regardless of the metric percentage

claim.text: The source says it does not really matter what the metrics are; if fundamental usability issues exist on the site, they should ultimately be resolved regardless of the percentage.
claim.quote: it doesn't really matter what the metrics are if there's usability issues fundamental that exist on the site ultimately you want to resolve them regardless of what the percentage is

action.text: When a fundamental usability issue is found on the site, resolve it even if the associated metric percentage is low.
action.quote: ultimately you want to resolve them regardless of what the percentage is

args.text: A fundamental usability issue exists on the site.
args.quote: if there's usability issues fundamental that exist on the site

unknowns: The source does not define what counts as a fundamental usability issue or how to verify resolution.

source.text: in this video I'm going to show you a complete in-depth tutorial on how to use Microsoft Clarity and all of the features available within the platform I'll show you not only how to use all of the features but also a complete tutorial on how to actually interpret the data within Clarity and if you stick towards the end of the video I'll show you real life examples and case studies of how we've used Clarity at our agency for our clients to increase their conversion rates getting right into it we have the main Clarity dashboard open up here so the first thing that I like to do when looking at the main dashboard is trying to filter for a good enough sample size or good enough sample period right so typically that's going to be the last 6 months of data it could also be last 90 days of data you know depending on when you set up Clarity you may or may not have the ability to go that far back so this might vary but you know 6 months is generally a good time period so I'm going to go back to January 2024 today's July 29th 2024 so roughly 6 months doesn't have to be exact and now I have all of the data available here so a lot of the metrics on the main Clarity dashboard you can actually pull directly from Google analytics so things like the scroll depth for example active time spent pages per session the total number of sessions these are all kind of Baseline kpis that you know doesn't really make Clarity unique in any regard like you can get this from other data sources the part that I find is important to focus on on the main dashboard is really this insights block here so we're looking at rage clicks dead clicks sucessive scrolling and then quick backs so rage clicks is the first one here which sits at 0 2% so this is actually people that are you know rage clicking or clicking multiple times on an element typically to kind of exit that experience so if you think about a like a website and you have a popup that lands immediately on the first 5 Seconds somebody's barely even scrolled on the site and they're just rage clicking trying to get rid of that popup you know that's where you'll typically find a lot of rage clicks right another use case might be where you know you're on a page and you're trying to exit a chat bot that's preventing you from adding to card or filling out a form and clicking the submit button if it's a B2B site right so again you know people are just trying to exit that and that's you know generally low hanging fruit opportunity what I like about Clarity is that you can actually click on this little camera icon and it's going to open up the recordings page where you can watch the actual recordings of people that experienced the rage clicks and later in the video we'll do a more in-depth walkth through of how to do recordings but for now we're just focusing on the main kpis so 0. 2% you know that's typically a pretty good rate I would say anything really under 1 to two% is good um but obviously these are low hanging food opportunities so if the rage clicks actually warrant particular change then it's worth watching those recordings to see you know where people experiencing frustration or friction the next thing is dead clicks so dead clicks is where somebody tries to click on an element then what happens is that element is actually not clickable hence the word dead right so normally what we see on client sites is you might have logos demonstrated on your your website and people think that those logos are clickable but they're actually not clickable right like if you have a ass featured on or ass seen on and people are trying to click on the logos right so that's an example of a dead click now in some scenarios dead clicks are fine because you might not want to send people outside right like the argument for as scen on or ass featured logos where you have places you've been featured in you might not necessarily want to send people outbound and outside of the website because your main goal is ultimately conversions if you're sending people outside they're not going to complete the the main action you want them to complete um so that's a scenario in which dead clicks are okay now there's the other scenario in which elements that should be clickable and that actually help people in their journey to complete a conversion is is not clickable so a good example of this would be this is uh actually an audit report that we do for our clients and this was an example where this is a SAS client so on their pricing section of their website they had a lot of clicks and movement registered around their pricing if you can see that on the right right so people thought that these elements were clickable but the only element that was actually clickable was the button that said get X number of free credits but you can see all of the other clicks that are registered in and around this area right and we'll get into this in the heat map part as well but this is an example of of dead clicks right where people think something's clickable it would actually benefit the the user a lot if they were clickable because people want to get the price but they're just clicking on things that you know are not designed to be clickable in the first place and hence that's going to increase the dead click rate another example of dead clicks would be this website here so when we went to the heat map tab uh what we noticed was that people were actually clicking on this logo uh in the center of the site and the logo wasn't even clickable like typically when you go on a website and you click on a logo it'll take you back to the homepage right most websites these days follow that convention but for some reason on the site the logo was not clickable and people were trying to click there from the checkout page from the product page to get back to the home but hence you know they couldn't and they were kind of Rage clicking and basically going through that dead click where it increased that percentage substantially and we noticed that on the main dashboard and we actually saw recordings of people as well right so dead clicks are super important uh and they're very useful okay so the next metric here is now excessive scrolling so excessive scrolling is when somebody is on a website and they're just scrolling very excessively on a particular page right so that just means they're going from top to bottom like very quickly um Clarity has certain metrics to identify this and typically what you can derive from this Insight is a couple different things it could be the fact that they're the user is trying to find information on the site but they can't find it right so for example they might be trying to look for reviews and you know they're just quickly scrolling through to try and find that information um another example might be they're trying to find a like a call to action Buton like the button to add to cart or the price of the product and it's nowhere to be found and they have to just scroll quickly to find it other use case might be you might have a long block of text that uh is just going throughout the entire page and I've seen examples of this so people are just completely skimming by it and going through the entire site uh to skip through it right so that's that's common use cases of excessive scrolling in this use case right now in this particular scenario it's less than 0.01% so it's not really a major concern and the last thing is Qui cck back so this is people where they're going to a page as cler saying right here and then they're quickly returning back to the previous one so this is normally derived the the Insight that can be derived from this is that you know people are looking for information on a page but they're not able to find it immediately right so they have to constantly bounce back and forth we'll typically notice this where somebody goes to like a page on the site and they're expecting certain information right for example a product page you'd expect to find certain information about the product but if you can't find it you're going to immediately go back right so that's also super important to understand and again I would consider watching the recordings of all of these um I know I kind of gave Baseline metrics for them but it doesn't really matter what the metrics are if there's usability issues fundamental that exist on the site ultimately you want to resolve them regardless of what the percentage is then as I scroll down there's a lot of different metrics here so you have Smart event so you can see different stages of the funnel this is a e-commerce site so I can see you know people that act to cart you can check out again you can do all of this inside of Google analytics and a much better job at that as well so I would really spend too much time there you can also see things like the refer the channel breakdown campaign Source again most of this you can do in uh GA and then you can see your browser data device Etc most popular Pages again a lot of this you can pretty much find inside of Google analytics so really the main piece of insight is the insights part of the dashboard okay so now we're going to segue over to the heat map portion of clarity I have a live demo count open up here for demonstration purposes where I'll actually walk through the data for the clarity website and this will give you a good idea of how to actually interpret the data that you're seeing so what I'll do is I'll click on the heat map tab up there and then I'll be presented with the most popular Pages since this is an example account you know there's only two pages that are listed here but typically you'll have 5 to 10 of the most popular Pages segmented by the volume of traffic that is coming to those pages but let's just click on the homepage here so the first thing I'm just going to mention is you might have a screenshot here that might existing_units.title: Watch recordings across all insight types regardless of the metric percentage

claim.text: The source says it does not really matter what the metrics are; fundamental usability issues existing on the site should be resolved regardless of the percentage.
claim.quote: it doesn't really matter what the metrics are if there's usability issues fundamental that exist on the site ultimately you want to resolve them regardless of what the percentage is

action.text: Watch the recordings behind all of the insight metrics, not only the ones with high rates.
action.quote: again I would consider watching the recordings of all of these

args.text: An insight metric looks low, for example excessive scrolling under 0.01 percent, and appears not to be a major concern.
args.quote: in this particular scenario it's less than 0.01% so it's not really a major concern

unknowns: The source does not define what counts as a fundamental usability issue or how resolution is verified.

existing_units.title: Understand dead clicks as clicks on elements that are not clickable

claim.text: Dead clicks are when somebody tries to click an element and that element is actually not clickable, hence the word dead.
claim.quote: dead clicks is where somebody tries to click on an element then what happens is that element is actually not clickable hence the word dead

unknowns: No dead-click rate threshold or benchmark is given in this passage.

existing_units.title: Some dead clicks are acceptable when linking out would cost conversions

claim.text: In some scenarios dead clicks are fine because the site may not want to send people outside.
claim.quote: in some scenarios dead clicks are fine because you might not want to send people outside

args.text: Clickable-looking elements such as as seen on or as featured logos risk sending users off-site.
args.quote: you might not necessarily want to send people outbound and outside of the website because your main goal is ultimately conversions

unknowns: The source frames this as an argument for keeping logos non-clickable, i.e. a judgement call rather than a rule.

existing_units.title: Other dead clicks are harmful when clickable elements would help conversion

claim.text: The other scenario is elements that should be clickable and that help people in their journey to conversion actually being not clickable.
claim.quote: there's the other scenario in which elements that should be clickable and that actually help people in their journey to complete a conversion is is not clickable

unknowns: The source does not state how to decide which elements should be clickable beyond the examples given.

existing_units.title: SaaS client pricing section registered dead clicks

claim.text: In a SaaS client audit, people thought pricing elements were clickable, but the only clickable element was the button for getting a number of free credits.
claim.quote: people thought that these elements were clickable but the only element that was actually clickable was the button that said get X number of free credits

unknowns: Client identity, dates, traffic volume and conversion impact are not stated in this passage.
The source adds that it would benefit users if those elements were clickable because people want the price, but the fix applied is not described.

existing_units.title: Non-clickable site logo produced dead clicks and rage clicks

existing_units.title: Read excessive scrolling as the user failing to find information

claim.text: Excessive scrolling can mean the user is trying to find information on the site but cannot find it.
claim.quote: it could be the fact that they're the user is trying to find information on the site but they can't find it

args.text: Excessive scrolling is recorded when a visitor scrolls a page top to bottom very quickly.
args.quote: excessive scrolling is when somebody is on a website and they're just scrolling very excessively on a particular page right so that just means they're going from top to bottom like very quickly

unknowns: Candidate causes given by the source are users hunting for reviews, hunting for a missing call to action or price, or skimming a long block of text; no rule for distinguishing them is stated.

existing_units.title: Avoid spending time on dashboard metrics Google Analytics already covers

reasons: The source supports using a roughly six-month period and says 90 days is another possible period, but it does not say to use 90 days specifically when less history exists. It only says historical availability may vary by when Clarity was set up.
The approximately six-month completion criterion is supported.
The substantive principle is supported: the speaker says the Insights block is the important part to focus on, while many listed KPIs are available in Google Analytics.
The asserted depends_on relation to date-range filtering is not established by the excerpt; the speaker presents filtering as a first practice, not as a prerequisite for prioritizing Insights.
The excerpt supports clicking the camera icon to open recordings and watching rage-click recordings when they may warrant a change.
The action overgeneralizes the demonstrated camera-icon behavior from rage clicks to any insight metric. This passage explicitly describes the icon and affected recordings for rage clicks only.
Its depends_on relation to the prior dashboard-prioritization principle is not stated.
The quoted heuristic that rates under 1 to 2 percent are good is supported and is correctly characterized as the speaker's own view.
The unknowns incorrectly describe the observed 0.2% rate as unreconciled with the under-1-to-2% heuristic. A 0.2% rate is compatible with that heuristic.
The source says the speaker would consider watching recordings for all listed insights and says fundamental usability issues should be resolved regardless of percentage.

The candidate turns a conditional recommendation into an unconditional instruction to watch all recordings. The source's qualification is that an actual fundamental usability issue should be resolved, not that every low-rate insight necessarily requires review.
The depends_on relation inherits the prior candidate's unsupported broad claim that the camera-icon workflow applies to all insight types.
The definition accurately reflects the excerpt: a dead click occurs when a user attempts to click an element that is not clickable.
No unsupported threshold, remedy, or platform behavior is added.
The source explicitly presents non-clickable featured-in logos as a scenario in which dead clicks may be acceptable because outbound navigation can conflict with conversion goals.
The candidate preserves the source's qualified framing rather than treating this as a universal rule.
The source explicitly contrasts acceptable dead clicks with elements that should be clickable because they assist the user's conversion journey.
The alternative relation to the prior, conversion-preserving scenario is consistent with the source's stated contrast.
The SaaS pricing example, including that only the free-credits button was clickable while users clicked surrounding pricing elements, is directly supported.
The candidate appropriately does not claim that a particular fix was implemented or that conversion results followed.
The excerpt supports that users clicked a non-clickable centered logo, including rage/dead-click behavior observed in dashboard data and recordings.
The candidate does not add an unsupported claim that the logo was subsequently fixed or that the fix had a measured effect.
The candidate retains the source's conditional interpretation: excessive scrolling can indicate that users cannot find information.
Its trigger correctly reflects the source's description of rapid top-to-bottom scrolling on a page.
The title and claimed warning infer that the speaker advises avoiding time on these metrics, but the quoted source clause is garbled: "so I would really spend too much time there."
The candidate itself acknowledges that a negation may be missing and that the polarity is unresolved. Therefore the excerpt cannot support the asserted avoidance recommendation.
The excerpt directly describes clicking the Heatmaps tab, being shown popular pages, and selecting the homepage in the demonstration.
The candidate accurately retains the distinction between the demo account's two pages and the speaker's statement that accounts typically show five to ten popular pages.
The candidate accurately identifies that the source ends mid-sentence while discussing heat-map screenshots and pop-ups.
It does not infer the missing pop-up effect, platform behavior, or remedy.

source_limitations: The supplied excerpt ends mid-sentence during the heat-map discussion, so the effect of pop-ups on screenshots and any recommended handling cannot be determined from this excerpt.
A purported recommendation about spending time on Google-Analytics-overlapping metrics contains a garbled clause with unresolved polarity: "so I would really spend too much time there."
The excerpt promises fuller recordings and heat-map walkthroughs later, but those procedures are not included here.

The excerpt provides illustrative observations and the speaker's heuristics, but does not provide a defined denominator for insight rates, a universal benchmark, or outcome data for the example fixes.
